lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Pipe welding is the backbone of Africa's growing infrastructure. From water pipelines in Kenya to oil and gas lines in Nigeria, welded pipes carry the fluids that keep industries and communities running. As a welder, mastering pipe welding opens doors to high-paying jobs in construction, mining, and energy. Unlike flat welding, pipe welding demands precision because pipes are round, and you often weld in fixed positionsâhorizontal, vertical, and overhead. In Africa, many projects require welding to international codes like AWS D10.10 or API 1104. Employers pay a premium for welders who can pass a 6G pipe test, which qualifies you to weld in any position. A certified pipe welder in South Africa can earn R300âR500 per hour, while in Nigeria, skilled pipe welders on oil rigs earn even more. This module will teach you the fundamentals: how to prepare pipes, select electrodes, control heat, and avoid defects. You'll learn using common tools like angle grinders, pipe stands, and welding machines (SMAW, GTAW, GMAW). We'll focus on carbon steel pipes, which are most common, but the principles apply to stainless and alloy pipes too. By the end, you'll be able to produce a sound root pass, hot pass, fill, and cap on a pipe joint. Remember, pipe welding is not just about making sparks; it's about creating a leak-proof, strong joint that can withstand pressure and corrosion. Whether you're working on a farm irrigation system or a cross-country pipeline, these skills are in demand. So let's get startedâyour ability to weld pipe can change your career.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To weld pipe properly, you need the right tools and materials. First, a welding machine: for stick welding (SMAW), a 200-amp inverter like the ESAB Rogue or Miller Thunderbolt is common in Africa. For TIG (GTAW), a machine with high-frequency start and foot pedal, such as the Everlast PowerTIG 200, works well. You'll also need an angle grinder with 4.5-inch or 9-inch discs for grinding tacks and cleaning. Pipe stands or rollers are essential to rotate pipes; you can make simple ones with steel pipes and bearings. For measurement, a pipe wrap-around (flexible tape) and a spirit level ensure proper alignment. Electrodes: for root passes on carbon steel, use E6010 or E6011 (cellulosic) for deep penetration, and E7018 for fill and cap. For TIG root, use ER70S-6 filler rod. Gas: for MIG (GMAW), use 75% Argon/25% CO2. For TIG, pure Argon. Safety gear: welding helmet with shade 10-13, leather gloves, flame-resistant jacket, and steel-toe boots. In Africa, you can source these from local welding suppliers or online from companies like Afrox, ESAB Africa, or local hardware stores. Pipe material: schedule 40 carbon steel pipes, 2-inch to 6-inch diameter, are ideal for practice. You'll also need a wire brush, chipping hammer, and soapstone or marker for marking. Don't forget a fire extinguisher and a bucket of water. A good workbench or welding table with a vise helps. If you're welding in the field, a portable generator (5-10 kW) powers your machine. Always check your cables and connections for wear. Having the right tools not only makes the job easier but also ensures safety and quality. Invest in good quality; cheap tools often fail and cause accidents.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps to weld a pipe joint in the 6G position (45-degree incline). First, prepare the pipe ends: cut them square, then bevel at 37.5 degrees using a grinder or pipe beveling machine. Clean the bevel and 1 inch around it with a grinder to bare metal. Tack weld four tacks at 12, 3, 6, and 9 o'clock positions using E6010 at 80-90 amps. Check alignment with a level and tape. Next, set your machine for root pass: E6010, DCEN (electrode negative), 70-90 amps. Start at the bottom (6 o'clock) and weld upward. Use a keyhole technique: push the electrode into the gap, create a keyhole, and move up, alternating side to side. Keep a tight arc and move quickly to avoid burn-through. After root, grind the start/stop to feather. For hot pass, use E7018 at 90-110 amps, DCEP, and weld over the root to fill any gaps. Then fill passes: E7018 at 100-120 amps, weave slightly to fill the groove. Finally, cap: E7018 at 100-120 amps, use a slight weave to create a convex bead. Clean each pass with a wire brush and chipping hammer. Check for defects like porosity or lack of fusion; grind out if needed. For TIG root, use ER70S-6 at 60-80 amps, DCEN, with a gas lens and 1/8-inch tungsten. Maintain a consistent travel speed. Practice on scrap pipes first. Remember, pipe welding is about consistency: keep your arc length short, angle correct (5-15 degrees drag), and travel speed steady. In Africa, many welders use the 'walking the cup' technique for TIG, but for stick, a slight weave works. Always test your welds with a bend test or visual inspection.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Pipe welding is unforgiving; small mistakes cause big failures. Here are common errors and how to fix them. 1) Burn-through: caused by too much heat, slow travel, or wide gap. Fix: reduce amps, increase travel speed, or use a smaller electrode. For root pass, try E6010 at lower amps (70-80) and a tighter gap. 2) Lack of penetration: happens when amps are too low, travel too fast, or bevel too narrow. Fix: increase amps, slow down, or widen bevel. Ensure the keyhole is visible. 3) Porosity: gas pockets from moisture, dirt, or windy conditions. Fix: clean pipe with grinder and acetone, use dry electrodes (bake E7018 at 250Â°C for 2 hours), and shield from wind with a welding blanket. 4) Slag inclusion: from not cleaning between passes. Fix: chip and brush thoroughly after each pass. 5) Undercut: from excessive weaving or high amps. Fix: reduce weave width, lower amps, or pause at edges. 6) Cracking: from rapid cooling or high sulfur in steel. Fix: preheat pipe to 100-150Â°C for thick sections, use E7018 (low hydrogen), and slow cooling. 7) Misalignment: from poor tacking. Fix: use a pipe clamp and check with a level before welding. 8) Arc blow: from magnetic fields. Fix: change ground position, use AC, or wrap cable around pipe. In Africa, humidity and dust are common culprits; store electrodes in a dry cabinet. Always inspect your work: a good weld is smooth, consistent, and free of holes. If you find a defect, grind it out and reweld. Don't try to cover it upâit will fail under pressure. Practice these fixes on scrap pipes until they become second nature.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Pipe welding carries serious hazards: burns, eye damage, fumes, and electric shock. Always wear a welding helmet with a proper shade (10-13 for stick, 9-13 for TIG), leather gloves, flame-resistant jacket, and steel-toe boots. Never weld in wet conditions or without proper ventilation. In Africa, many workshops are open-air; if welding outdoors, use a welding screen to protect others from arc flash. Fumes from welding can cause metal fume fever; use a respirator if welding galvanized or stainless steel. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby and a bucket of sand or water. Before welding, inspect your machine and cables for damage; replace worn cables. Ground the workpiece directly to the pipe, not to the table, to avoid shock. Use a dry wooden board or rubber mat to stand on. When welding pipe, secure it properly on stands to prevent rolling. Never weld a pressurized pipe or one containing flammable residue. For best practice, follow these steps: 1) Plan your weld: know the position, electrode, and amps. 2) Clean the pipe and fit-up correctly. 3) Use the right technique for each pass. 4) Inspect after each pass. 5) Keep your work area tidy. 6) Stay hydratedâwelding in hot African climates can cause heat stress. 7) Take breaks to avoid fatigue, which leads to mistakes. 8) Learn first aid for burns and eye injuries. 9) Always use the correct polarity: DCEN for E6010 root, DCEP for E7018. 10) Practice on scrap until you're confident. Remember, safety is not just for you but for everyone around you. A safe welder is a productive welder.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to put your skills to the test. This exercise will guide you through welding a 2-inch schedule 40 carbon steel pipe in the 6G position. You'll need: two pieces of pipe, each 6 inches long, beveled at 37.5 degrees, with a 1/8-inch root gap. You'll also need your welding machine (SMAW), E6010 and E7018 electrodes, grinder, wire brush, chipping hammer, and safety gear. Set up the pipes on stands at a 45-degree angle. Tack weld at four points with E6010 at 80 amps. Check alignment. For the root pass, use E6010 at 75 amps, DCEN. Start at 6 o'clock and weld upward, using a keyhole technique. Aim for a consistent bead with slight penetration inside. After root, grind the start and stop. For hot pass, use E7018 at 95 amps, DCEP, and weld over the root. Then fill passes: E7018 at 110 amps, weaving slightly. Finally, cap: E7018 at 110 amps, with a slight weave to cover the groove. Clean between each pass. After welding, let the pipe cool, then inspect visually. Look for uniform ripple pattern, no undercut, no porosity. If you have a grinder, cut the pipe longitudinally to check penetration. You should see full fusion at the root. If defects are found, note them and practice again. For a more advanced challenge, try TIG root with ER70S-6 at 70 amps, then stick fill and cap. Repeat this exercise at least five times, varying positions (2G, 5G, 6G). In Africa, many welders practice on scrap pipes from local suppliers. Record your settings and results in a notebook. This exercise builds muscle memory and confidence. Once you can consistently produce a sound weld, you're ready for certification tests. Remember, practice makes permanentâso practice correctly.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pipe Welding Fundamentals for African Agribusiness & Fabrication Enterprises

Pipe welding is the backbone of profitable fabrication work across Africa â from irrigation manifolds on a 40-hectare tomato farm in Nigeria, to borehole pump columns in Kenya, to milk-transfer lines in a Rwandan dairy, to fuel and water reticulation for a Zambian poultry operation. For an African agribusiness, welding is not just a technical skill: it is a revenue line, a maintenance capability, and a risk-management tool. This practical reference consolidates the tools, materials, methods, defects, safety rules, and a field-ready checklist for welders working on carbon steel and stainless pipe in agricultural and agro-processing settings.

Work through this module alongside the earlier lessons (Introduction and Why It Matters, Tools and Materials, Step by Step Method, Common Mistakes and Fixes, Safety and Best Practice, and the Practical Exercise). The goal is simple: produce leak-free, code-conscious pipe joints that keep water, fuel, milk, and process fluids flowing â and keep your enterprise earning.

Table 1: Pipe Welding Process Selection Matrix (Africa Field Conditions)

Process Best for (typical agri use) Power supply / site needs Typical pipe wall (mm) Relative cost & skill
SMAW (stick) Borehole columns, irrigation mains, fuel lines, repairs Portable inverter 200 A; single-phase or generator 3â12 Low cost / moderate skill
GTAW (TIG) Stainless milk/process lines, thin-wall hygiene tubing AC/DC TIG; clean, dry, low-dust environment 1.5â6 Higher cost / high skill
GMAW (MIG) Fabrication shop pipe spools, structural pipe frames 230/400 V; shielding gas (COâ/Ar mix) supply chain limited in rural areas 3â10 Medium cost / moderate skill
FCAW (flux-core) Heavy pipe, outdoor repairs, windy sites Higher current; robust against wind 6â20 Medium cost / moderate skill

Source: Adapted from Lincoln Electric, Pipe Welding Procedures (free technical PDF, lincolnelectric.com) and AWS Welding Handbook, Vol. 1 & 2 (aws.org). Site-need column reflects common African rural agribusiness power realities (grid instability, generator dependence).

Table 2: Common Pipe Weld Defects, Causes & Business Impact

Defect Main cause Field detection Business impact if missed
Lack of penetration (LOP) Root gap too small; low current; fast travel Hydrostatic test; visual root inspection Leaks, pump cavitation, crop water loss
Porosity Damp electrodes; dirty/damp pipe; wind on GMAW Visual; dye penetrant (PT) Rework cost, downtime during peak season
Slag inclusion Poor interpass cleaning (SMAW/FCAW) Visual; radiography (RT) on critical lines Premature failure, warranty claims
Undercut Excessive current; wrong angle; long arc Visual; pipe-wall micrometer Reduced wall thickness â burst risk
Burn-through Root gap too large; too much current on thin wall Visual; leak test Scrap spool, wasted material & labour
Cracking (HAZ) Fast cooling; high carbon/hydrogen; poor fit-up PT; visual after cooling Catastrophic failure, safety incident, reputational loss

Source: Compiled from AWS D10.12M/D10.12 (aws.org), Lincoln Electric Pipe Welding Procedures, and ESAB Pipe Welding Guide (free PDF, esab.com).

â  SAFETY WARNING â CONFINED SPACE & FUME HAZARD:

Never weld inside a pipe, tank, pit, or borehole chamber without a trained standby person, continuous forced ventilation, atmospheric testing (Oâ, flammable gas, HâS), and a rescue plan. Welding fumes from galvanised, painted, or stainless pipe can cause metal-fume fever and long-term lung damage. In African field conditions, generators and inverters must be earthed (grounded) and fitted with an RCD/earth-leakage device. Arc eye, burns, and electrocution in wet conditions are the most common serious injuries â wear a welding helmet with correct shade (min. shade 10 for SMAW), leather gloves, apron, and safety boots at all times. Follow your country's Occupational Health & Safety Act (e.g., Kenya OSHA 2007, South Africa OHSA Act 85 of 1993, Nigeria Factories Act).

Quick Reference Checklist (Field-Ready)

  1. Verify materials: Confirm pipe grade (e.g., ASTM A53/A106 carbon steel, ASTM A312 stainless), diameter, and wall thickness match the drawing and the fluid (water, fuel, milk, slurry).
  2. Check power & consumables: Confirm generator/inverter output, electrode type (e.g., E6010 root, E7018 fill/cap), and that electrodes are dry (re-bake if damp).
  3. Fit-up & tack: Bevel at 30Â°â37.5Â°, root gap 1.5â3 mm, root face 1â2 mm; use 3â4 tacks, aligned and ground thin.
  4. Root pass: Weld with correct current and travel speed to achieve full penetration without burn-through; inspect root where accessible.
  5. Clean every pass: Remove slag, spatter, and oxides before the next pass â especially on stainless (use a dedicated stainless brush).
  6. Control heat & cooling: Manage interpass temperature; avoid quenching; allow controlled cooling to prevent HAZ cracking.
  7. Inspect & test: Visual inspection, then hydrostatic or pneumatic leak test (follow pressure limits); use PT/RT on critical or high-value lines.
  8. Record & hand over: Log welder ID, process, consumables, and test result â essential for warranty, insurance, and future maintenance.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • Lincoln Electric â Education & Training (free pipe welding procedures and guides)
  • ESAB â Technical Documentation & Pipe Welding Guides (free PDFs)
  • American Welding Society (AWS) â D10 Committee Pipe & Tube Welding Standards
  • OSHA â Welding, Cutting & Brazing Safety Guidance (free)
  • ILO â Occupational Safety & Health resources (free, relevant to African workplaces)

Business takeaway: In African agribusiness, a certified pipe welder with a documented procedure reduces water loss, fuel leakage, milk contamination, and unplanned downtime â all of which directly hit the bottom line. Treat every pipe joint as a profit-critical asset, not just a technical task.

quiz.q: What is the primary reason pipe welding is important in Africa?
options: A) It is easier than flat welding
B) It is needed for infrastructure like pipelines
D) It is only for oil rigs
quiz.explanation: Pipe welding is crucial for building and maintaining pipelines and other infrastructure across Africa.

quiz.q: Which welding position is considered the most challenging?
quiz.explanation: The 6G position combines all positions and is used for certification tests.

quiz.q: What does a 6G pipe test qualify a welder to do?
options: A) Weld only in flat position
C) Weld only pipes under 2 inches
quiz.explanation: A 6G certification allows welding in all positions on pipe.

quiz.q: Which electrode is commonly used for the root pass on carbon steel pipe?
quiz.explanation: E6010 is a cellulosic electrode that provides deep penetration for root passes.

quiz.q: What is the recommended bevel angle for pipe welding?
quiz.explanation: A 37.5-degree bevel is standard for pipe welding to ensure proper penetration.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to check pipe alignment?
quiz.explanation: A spirit level ensures the pipe is properly aligned before welding.

quiz.q: What polarity is used for E6010 root pass?
quiz.explanation: E6010 runs best on DCEN (electrode negative) for deep penetration.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a hot pass?
options: A) To fill the groove completely
C) To fill any gaps and reinforce the root
quiz.explanation: The hot pass fills any voids and reinforces the root pass.

quiz.q: Which electrode is used for fill and cap passes?
quiz.explanation: E7018 is a low-hydrogen electrode ideal for fill and cap passes.

quiz.q: What causes burn-through in pipe welding?
options: B) Too high amperage or slow travel
quiz.explanation: Excessive heat from high amps or slow travel can burn through the pipe.

quiz.q: How can you prevent porosity in pipe welds?
options: C) Clean the pipe and use dry electrodes
quiz.explanation: Porosity is often caused by moisture, dirt, or wind, so cleaning and dry electrodes help.

quiz.q: What is slag inclusion and how is it fixed?
options: A) Gas pockets; fix by welding faster
B) Trapped slag; fix by cleaning between passes
D) Undercut; fix by reducing amps
quiz.explanation: Slag inclusion occurs when slag is trapped in the weld; cleaning between passes prevents it.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of undercut?
options: B) Excessive weaving or high amps
quiz.explanation: Undercut happens when the arc melts the base metal edges excessively, often from too much heat or weave.

quiz.q: How can you prevent cracking in pipe welds?
options: B) Preheat thick sections and use low-hydrogen electrodes
C) Use E6010 for all passes
quiz.explanation: Preheating and low-hydrogen electrodes reduce the risk of cracking.

quiz.q: What is arc blow and how is it fixed?
options: A) Arc wandering due to magnetic fields; fix by changing ground position
B) Arc going out; fix by increasing amps
C) Arc too short; fix by lengthening
D) Arc too long; fix by shortening
quiz.explanation: Arc blow is caused by magnetic forces and can be fixed by relocating the ground or using AC.

quiz.q: Why should you bake E7018 electrodes?
options: B) To remove moisture and prevent porosity
quiz.explanation: Baking removes moisture, which can cause porosity in welds.

quiz.q: What safety gear is essential for pipe welding?
options: B) Welding helmet, gloves, flame-resistant jacket, and boots
quiz.explanation: Full protective gear is necessary to prevent burns, eye damage, and electric shock.

quiz.q: What should you do before welding a pipe?
options: B) Clean the pipe and fit-up correctly
quiz.explanation: Proper cleaning and fit-up are crucial for a quality weld.

quiz.q: What is the correct shade for a welding helmet when stick welding?
quiz.explanation: Shade 10-13 is recommended for stick welding to protect eyes from arc rays.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important in pipe welding?
options: A) To keep the welder cool
quiz.explanation: Welding fumes can be toxic, so proper ventilation is necessary.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical exercise?
options: B) Prepare and bevel the pipe ends
quiz.explanation: Preparation includes cutting and beveling the pipe ends before welding.

quiz.q: How many tacks are typically used for a pipe joint?
quiz.explanation: Four tacks at 12, 3, 6, and 9 o'clock positions are standard.

quiz.q: What technique is used for the root pass with E6010?
quiz.explanation: The keyhole technique ensures full penetration in the root pass.

quiz.q: What should you do after completing each pass?
options: A) Immediately weld the next pass
B) Clean with a wire brush and chipping hammer
quiz.explanation: Cleaning between passes prevents slag inclusion and ensures good fusion.

quiz.q: How can you check penetration after welding?
quiz.explanation: Cutting the pipe allows you to see if the root has full penetration.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for E6010 root pass on 2-inch pipe?
quiz.explanation: 70-90 amps is typical for E6010 root pass on thin pipe.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a cap pass?
options: B) To cover the weld and provide a smooth finish
quiz.explanation: The cap pass covers the fill passes and gives the weld its final shape.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when welding in windy conditions?
quiz.explanation: Wind can blow away shielding gas, causing porosity in the weld.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid welding on a pressurized pipe?
options: B) It can cause an explosion
D) It is not allowed by code
quiz.explanation: Welding a pressurized pipe can lead to rupture or explosion.

quiz.q: What is the best way to practice pipe welding?
options: A) Only weld in flat position
B) Practice on scrap pipes in various positions
quiz.explanation: Hands-on practice on scrap pipes in different positions builds skill.
